items.title: Regulation in the Digital Information Space
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) tools and digital platforms become embedded in everyday communication, governments face growing pressure to regulate misinformation, hate speech, and other harmful online content while protecting freedom of expression. This study examines regulatory debates in Mongolia’s digital information space and argues that regulatory acceptance and legitimacy cannot be explained through an individual-centered perspective alone. It first organizes Mongolia’s digital governance challenges through four interrelated forms of uncertainty: cultural, ethical, institutional, and relational. This approach highlights Mongolia’s hybrid cultural environment, where collectivist traditions intersect with expanding individualism, and where public judgments about regulation are shaped by relationships and trust. Drawing on a quota-sampling survey of two hundred and seventy respondents from urban and rural Mongolia, the study employs Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and multi-group analysis to examine the direct, mediating, and moderating effects of four trust dimensions: strong-tie trust, weak-tie trust, institutional trust, and platform trust. The findings show that institutional trust is the strongest positive predictor of regulatory acceptance, followed by platform trust, strong-tie trust, and weak-tie trust. Relational trust statistically mediates the relationship between freedom-of-expression concerns and regulatory acceptance, suggesting that concerns about censorship are interpreted through broader trust environments. Urban-rural and generational differences further condition the effects of trust. The Mongolian case illustrates broader challenges faced by small democracies and platform-dependent societies, where domestic regulatory capacity remains limited while global platforms shape the public sphere. The study demonstrates the need to understand regulatory legitimacy through relationships, trust, and cultural context, not solely legal systems or individual literacy alone.

items.title: RegulaTutor: A Theory-Informed Framework for Long-Term Personalized Learning
items.abstract: Long-term personalized tutoring requires language models to translate a learner's evolving history into appropriate instructional support. Existing LLM-based tutoring systems use memory and retrieval to personalize responses, but the pedagogical rationale linking historical evidence to teaching strategies is not always explicit. We introduce RegulaTutor, a theory-informed framework for long-term personalized tutoring that connects historical evidence, learner interpretation, and learner-facing instruction. Guided by self-regulated learning (SRL) research, its tutoring harness operationalizes a cognitive, affective, metacognitive, and motivational (CAMM) framework for deriving evidence-supported learner interpretations and teaching policies. The resulting policies retain links to their supporting evidence and are updated as new observations arrive. This staged workflow also supports systematic refinement through PairRoute, an offline procedure that uses intermediate execution records to distinguish harness, model, and mixed failures. PairRoute proposes and evaluates targeted harness revisions, then constructs reviewed stage-level supervision for confirmed model failures remaining under the selected harness. We focus this refinement on historical evidence acquisition, which underpins personalized instruction and allows outputs to be checked against learning records and reference answers. RegulaTutor improves historical-evidence accuracy, learner diagnosis, and judged teaching quality on average across evaluated model configurations. PairRoute results show an endpoint improvement in standalone-model historical-evidence accuracy over the refinement trajectory. Together, these results highlight RegulaTutor's potential to support lifelong personalized education through instructional policies that evolve with learner histories and targeted improvements to the tutoring system.

items.title: Relational Role Attribution: A Unifying Construct in Human–AI Interaction
items.abstract: How users come to perceive an AI not merely as capable but as intentionally oriented toward them in a specific relational capacity remains undertheorized. We propose relational role attribution (RRA) as a discrete psychological construct addressing this gap, positioned as a precursor to downstream relational outcomes rather than a reframing of trust. A PRISMA-ScR scoping review charted 1223 reports at full text against a registered protocol, including 466. Of 179 records excluded for establishing no relational or social role for the agent, 122 (68.2%) nonetheless manipulated or measured anthropomorphism: the field reaches the cue and stops short of the attribution. RRA comprises two concurrent components, a relational inference of social orientation and a role assignment drawn from contextual and communicative cues, checked against the expectancy the user brings. Naming the attribution allows findings accumulated separately across marketing, teaming, and communication literatures to constrain one another, and scaffolds role-specific design principles.

items.title: Repositioning the role of information and communication technologies and artificial intelligence in the fight against human trafficking
items.abstract: Despite decades of international commitment under anti-trafficking law and policy frameworks, such efforts to combat human trafficking have struggled to keep pace with its rapidly evolving digital dimensions. Artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies remain underused in anti-trafficking strategies, while perpetrators exploit them with speed and sophistication. Drawing on findings from the Horizon Europe VANGUARD project, this chapter examines why current approaches fall short and how responsibly designed technology could enhance responses. This chapter presents research which identifies persistent shortcomings: reliance on reactive law enforcement, fragmented data ecosystems, limited survivor involvement, algorithmic bias, surveillance misuse, and insufficient adaptation to the fluid online dynamics of trafficking for labour and sexual exploitation, as well as forced criminality. In response, VANGUARD developed a suite of AI-enabled tools, co-created with stakeholders, to anticipate and disrupt digital trafficking pathways. However, as underlined in this chapter, the VANGUARD research makes it clear that technology alone is insufficient. Without systemic reforms, innovation risks reproducing existing injustices. This chapter calls for evidence-based, ethically grounded, user-centred strategies, supported by survivor-informed observatories, cross-sector collaboration, and ongoing research into perpetrator behaviour, digital infrastructures, and structural drivers of exploitation.

items.title: Research on the Cultivation Path of Students' Critical Thinking in Management Consulting Courses under AI Empowerment
items.abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence has restructured the working models and talent demand standards of the management consulting industry. As an essential advanced competency for management consulting professionals, critical thinking equips practitioners and students to analyze AI-generated consulting results, address complex managerial issues. Based on AI technology application scenarios, this paper analyzes the current dilemmas in cultivating critical thinking in undergraduate management consulting courses, constructs a cultivation system covering four dimensions—teaching objectives, teaching content, teaching models, and evaluation mechanisms—and explores curriculum education pathways adapted to the AI era. This study seeks to develop students’ capabilities in consulting critical thinking, problem analysis, and intelligent tool mastery, providing references for the intelligent teaching reform of economics and management majors and the cultivation of higher-order thinking talents.

items.title: Researcher-Driven Insights for Human-Agent Teaming Testbeds
items.abstract: Human-Agent Teaming (HAT) is becoming increasingly important as AI systems take on collaborative roles. However, HAT research depends on experimental testbeds to study human-agent teams. This research builds on prior work that cataloged existing HAT testbeds by identifying and characterizing user needs for future HAT testbeds. In this study, nine HAT researchers were interviewed about their experimental design practices and testbed usage. Affinity diagramming was used to identify themes about pain points with existing testbeds and user needs for future testbeds. Participants indicated growing interest in using AI technologies in testbeds, to design experiments or serve as realistic teammates. Participants emphasized the importance of agent-agnostic testbeds that enable integration with external agents. These findings inform requirements for more flexible HAT testbeds that address current limitations and accommodate future research directions.

items.title: Residual Atherogenic Dyslipidemia in Normal-Weight Adults: The Role of Visceral Adiposity and Metabolic Dysfunction
items.abstract: Background. Body mass index (BMI) remains the most widely used tool for obesity classification and cardiometabolic risk stratification. However, increasing evidence suggests that normal BMI does not necessarily reflect metabolic health, particularly in individuals with hidden visceral adiposity and residual atherogenic dyslipidemia. The present study aimed to evaluate the prevalence of residual atherogenic dyslipidemia among normal-weight adults and to analyze its association with visceral adiposity, metabolic dysfunction, and lifestyle-related factors. Methods. A cross-sectional observational study was conducted in 166,008 Spanish workers aged 18–69 years with normal BMI (18.5–24.9 kg/m2) who underwent standardized occupational health examinations between 2022 and 2024. Anthropometric, biochemical, vascular, and lifestyle-related variables were evaluated. Visceral adiposity was estimated using waist-to-height ratio (WtHR) and the Metabolic Score for Visceral Fat (METS-VF). Residual atherogenic dyslipidemia was primarily assessed using the triglyceride-to-HDL cholesterol ratio (TG/HDL-c). Multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify independent associations with elevated TG/HDL-c. Results. Despite normal BMI values, 8.0% of participants presented with an elevated TG/HDL-c ratio, 11.8% had central adiposity, 11.4% showed low HDL cholesterol, and 17.9% exhibited elevated blood pressure. Individuals with an elevated TG/HDL-c ratio demonstrated significantly higher waist circumference, WtHR, METS-VF, triglycerides, non-HDL cholesterol, fasting glucose, blood pressure, and TyG index values (all p < 0.001). A progressive worsening of lipid and metabolic parameters was observed across increasing METS-VF quartiles. Elevated TG/HDL-c ratio prevalence increased from 2.7% in the lowest METS-VF quartile to 15.8% in the highest quartile. Men showed a substantially higher prevalence of residual atherogenic dyslipidemia than women (12.2% vs. 3.9%, p < 0.001). Physical inactivity, smoking, poor Mediterranean diet adherence, and regular alcohol consumption were strongly associated with adverse lipid-metabolic profiles. In multivariable analyses using separate adiposity measures, BMI and METS-VF remained independently associated with elevated TG/HDL-c, whereas WtHR ≥ 0.50 was not independently associated after adjustment. Male sex, physical inactivity, smoking, impaired fasting glucose, elevated blood pressure, and low Mediterranean diet adherence showed consistent associations across models. Conclusions. Residual atherogenic dyslipidemia is highly prevalent among adults with normal BMI and is strongly associated with visceral adiposity, metabolic dysfunction, and unfavorable lifestyle-related behaviors. Conventional BMI classification alone substantially underestimates hidden cardiometabolic risk. These findings highlight the metabolic heterogeneity present among apparently healthy normal-weight individuals and the limitations of BMI as a sole marker of cardiometabolic health.

items.title: Responsibility closure in healthcare shift handover: A systematic review and SEIPS 2.0-informed framework synthesis
items.abstract: • Responsibility closure shifts handover assessment to each unfinished obligation. • Five conditions distinguish nominal transfer from executable continuity. • Communication improvements often outpace evidence on follow-through and safety. • Work-system capacity is part of credible responsibility transfer. • The framework is provisional and requires prospective validation. Healthcare shift handovers are commonly evaluated as information-transfer events, yet patient safety also depends on whether unfinished work is understood, assigned and executable within the receiving system. We systematically reviewed empirical studies of real healthcare shift-boundary handovers and developed a provisional SEIPS 2.0-informed integrative framework for analysing this operational endpoint. PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection and OpenAlex were searched through 13 July 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching. Screening, eligibility assessment, extraction, MMAT appraisal and synthesis were conducted by the primary reviewer, with independent verification of prespecified samples across review stages. From 2,876 identified records, 172 reports representing 167 independent studies were included. Best-fit framework synthesis identified five analytically distinguishable conditions relevant to credible responsibility closure: visibility of unfinished work; active reception and shared understanding; actionability and priority; explicit ownership; and operational capacity. Intervention studies more consistently reported improvements in communication completeness and documentation, whereas ownership, subsequent action and patient-safety outcomes were less frequently and less robustly evaluated. Responsibility closure describes the obligation-level state in which consequential unfinished work has an identifiable receiving location, a feasible next action and sufficient capacity for action or escalation. It therefore extends beyond information completeness or nominal transfer of accountability by requiring operational executability. The evidence was heterogeneous, predominantly healthcare-based and did not directly validate the construct or its candidate indicators. Responsibility closure offers a provisional systems-oriented framework for designing and evaluating handovers around the continuation of unfinished work. Prospective studies should test its association with follow-through, delay, escalation and harm.

items.abstract: Generative AI increasingly supports clinical diagnosis and prognosis, but safe deployment into clinical practice requires standardized evaluation. Current automated and human evaluation methods rely heavily on accuracy, lack multimodal assessment, and are not aligned with human judgment. Emerging benchmarks are assessed and linked to our framework. A hybrid evaluation approach combining automated scalability with expert clinical judgment is recommended for safe and effective deployment.

items.title: Retrieval‐Augmented Lesson Generation With Large Language Models for Scenario‐Based Tutor Training
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background High‐impact tutoring can improve student learning, but scaling tutoring programmes requires large numbers of novice tutors. Developing high‐quality tutor‐training lessons remains a key bottleneck. Objectives This study compared post‐test performance after participants studied human‐created or LLM‐created tutor‐training materials and examined whether immediate explanatory feedback moderated differences by lesson creation source (human‐created vs. LLM‐created). Methods We conducted a randomized eight‐condition between‐subjects experiment. Participants completed a source‐matched pre‐instruction practice assessment, studied a tutor‐training lesson created by the same source, and then completed two fixed‐order post‐lesson assessments. The design compared lesson creation source, manipulated immediate explanatory feedback and counterbalanced the pre‐instruction scenario form. Post‐test performance was the mean proportion correct across the human‐created and LLM‐created post‐lesson assessments. Results and Conclusions Average post‐test performance was higher after the human‐created lesson than after the LLM‐created lesson, but this difference depended on feedback. The human‐created advantage appeared in the no‐feedback condition, whereas no statistically reliable lesson creation source difference was detected when feedback was provided. Feedback had no statistically significant overall main effect. The human‐created lesson condition performed better on the human‐created post‐lesson assessment, while the LLM‐created post‐lesson assessment showed a small descriptive difference favouring the LLM‐created lesson condition. Because pre‐instruction performance differed by lesson creation source and scenario form, and because assessment source was confounded with fixed assessment order, the results do not isolate pure learning gains or establish a general transfer advantage.

items.title: Revisiting the Task of Building Damage Assessment by Satellite Imaging
items.abstract: Natural disasters such as earthquakes, tropical storms, and floods cause extensive damage to buildings, and rapid, reliable damage maps are essential to guide emergency response. Automating this task, referred to as building damage assessment (BDA), from satellite imagery, has become an active research topic at the intersection of remote sensing, computer vision, and machine learning, particularly since supervised deep learning methods were shown to outperform earlier handcrafted approaches. Yet, despite a decade of intense activity and the release of several large-scale datasets, the field lacks a shared foundation. This chapter revisits the task of BDA from first principles, organized around three pillars: data, evaluation, and methods. We first clarify the candidate task for- mulations and argue for a sensor-agnostic, instance-based definition that tolerates missing pre-event imagery. We then review existing datasets along the axes of sensing modality, temporal configuration, and geographic coverage. On the evaluation side, we show that prevailing practices, largely based on a single aggregate score, are theoretically fragile, and we lay the foundations of a more informative, ranking-based, multi-score protocol. We further review methods ranging from task-specific deep networks to recent Earth observation foundation models, noticing that generalization to unseen events and regions remains an open difficulty. Finally, we discuss how these elements can inform the organization of a BDA challenge, including cross-validation, challenge, and private data-sharing setups designed to build trust between developers and users.

items.title: Roadmap to Fully Closing the Loop to Optimize Health in Type 1 Diabetes
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Current commercially available automated insulin delivery systems require meal and exercise announcements for optimal function, placing them in the hybrid closed loop category. Ongoing advancements aim to establish fully closed loop (FCL) systems as the next-generation standard for type 1 diabetes (T1D) management, eliminating the need for such inputs. We sought to develop a shared definition of FCL so that emerging technologies, including those using artificial intelligence, multi-hormone delivery, multi-analyte sensing, and/or adjunctive therapies, are held to uniform performance standards. METHODS: A group of invited experts, including clinicians, researchers, and people with lived experience convened to propose an outcome-driven definition of FCL systems. RESULTS: FCL systems are defined by three core domains centered on meeting intensive glycemic targets while reducing self-management burden and improving lived experience: Time in Tight Range (TITR) 70-140 mg/dL (3.9-7.8 mmol/L), Time Below Range (TBR) <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L), and person-reported outcomes (PROs) measured with validated T1D-specific assessments. This definition rests on a three-tiered classification in which all FCL systems improve lived experience and attain >50% TITR and <1% TBR without mandatory meal or activity announcements. Class 3 systems must attain >50% TITR; Class 2, >70%; and Class 1, >90%-while simultaneously demonstrating improved quality of life and reduced treatment burden per validated PROs. Given the elevated hypoglycemia risk from insulin-on-board during exercise, Class 1a requires >90% TITR with demonstrable hypoglycemia prevention during standardized exercise testing (0% TBR). CONCLUSION: This framework provides a uniform benchmark for evaluating future FCL technologies. Taken together, this person-centered, outcome-driven framework holds that FCL systems should (1) autonomously attain near-normoglycemia, (2) meaningfully improve lived experience across the lifespan and clinical contexts, and (3) prevent exercise-related hypoglycemia.

items.title: Robotics for Aging Populations
items.abstract: Robotics offers versatile tools to face the challenges due to the older population growth, especially meeting the needs for assisting the elderly in the activities of daily living (ADLs) and for the geriatric care. However, the perspectives offered by human factors studies can further enhance this potential of robotics. This chapter explores the integration of ergonomics in the design of robots devised to enhance the independence and well-being of older adults. Furthermore, we mention the opportunities offered by wearable robotics, telepresence, and the pervasive solutions of the Internet of Robotic Things (IoRT) to implement paradigms of precision healthcare with decentralized and ubiquitous features, improving the sustainability of elderly care—following the human-centric perspectives of Society 5.0 and Health 5.0, with their synergies. For instance, we discuss issues of technology acceptance alongside the perspectives of value-sensitive design to ensure that robotics align with the experiential and, in particular, ethical needs in aging people and communities, first of all for inclusion. Intelligent systems will also be discussed for their potential to make robotic solutions even more versatile and adjustable to the seniors’ needs. By prioritizing the needs and preferences of older individuals (and their own network of relatives, friends, and acquaintances), ergonomics in robotics must contribute to the societal mission of preserving dignity, autonomy, and quality of life in aging societies.

items.title: Robust Vision-Language Navigation with Awareness of Instruction-Execution Progress
items.abstract: In Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) tasks involving multi-step instructions as guidance, an agent must associate its observations with the relevant instruction content at each decision point. Most graph-based methods commonly match candidate trajectories with the entire instruction, allowing already executed content to interfere with subsequent decisions. Although instruction-execution progress provides a direct cue for separating executed and pending content, existing progress estimation approaches often rely on explicit progress supervision, sophisticated progress-learning stages, or costly online reasoning with LLMs. In this paper, we propose a robust VLN framework with Awareness of Instruction-Execution Progress (VLN-AIEP), which couples progress estimation with navigation decision-making. VLN-AIEP associates the visited trajectory with the instruction to suppress embeddings corresponding to executed content, and then matches candidate locations with the pending content. This coupling makes correct navigation decisions depend on accurate progress estimation, allowing the progress estimator to learn directly from navigation decision labels without explicit progress annotations. To support progress estimation, we construct a landmark-anchored trajectory representation that encodes the semantic labels and viewpoint-relative geometry of instruction-referred landmarks. These landmarks serve as spatial references for associating the visited trajectory with executed instruction content. Extensive experiments on R2R, RxR, CVDN, and R2R-CE demonstrate that the proposed method achieves favorable performance across multiple metrics.

items.title: Rollout-Time Intervention: Unlocking Agentic Reinforcement Learning Beyond Policy Limits
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) agents, enabling stronger reasoning, planning, and tool-use in interactive environments. However, existing agent RL methods remain fundamentally constrained by an on-policy reasoning bottleneck: when tasks exceed the model's current capability boundary, effective trajectories become extremely sparse and training often collapses. We introduce Rollout-Time Intervention (RTI), a technique designed to elicit successful trajectories beyond the policy's intrinsic exploration capacity. RTI operates by leveraging reward-side evidence (i.e., evaluation rubrics) during rollout to convert erroneous trajectories into successful ones, providing effective learning signals for tasks that the policy rarely solves on its own. Although intervention trajectories are inherently off-policy, we find that they can effectively guide policy optimization when trajectories with excessive distributional shifts are filtered out. Extensive experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that RTI consistently outperforms RL baselines, enabling the post-trained policy to approach the performance of substantially stronger contemporary LLMs and, more importantly, transcend its original capability boundary. The code is available at https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/qqr.

items.title: Same Query, Different Answer: Run-to-Run Variance in Semantic Query Processing
items.abstract: Semantic query engines ask a large language model (LLM) to judge individual rows, and benchmarks compare these engines on the quality of a few executions at temperature 0. We measure how much another execution changes. We re-execute the text and tabular workloads of SemBench, LRO-Bench, and UDA-Bench through their own harnesses, log every one of 1.2 million model calls, and reanalyze SemBench's published executions. At temperature 0, between 0.07% and 10.2% of rows change their operator output over five executions, depending on the model, and up to 24.0% on one task. Plans amplify these changes exponentially in the number of rows an answer exposes, as a possible-worlds model predicts: on UDA-Bench, a few percent of extracted values change, but about two thirds of the answers do. In SemBench's published results, 21% of text results change quality between executions, including on engines whose plans are deterministic. Changing rows are rows on which models disagree with each other; identical requests within one execution disagree as often as across executions; and one execution's decision margin or reasoning length predicts which rows change. Voting reduces the variance but does not remove it, and a calibrated cascade keeps its guarantee while the rows it returns change. We derive reporting rules for benchmarks and design rules for engines.

items.title: SAMWater: a prompt-guided multimodal framework for transferable water mapping with the segment anything model
items.abstract: Accurate and transferable surface water mapping is critical for water resource assessment, flood monitoring, and aquatic ecosystem management, but remains difficult because SAR speckle, optical contamination, heterogeneous backgrounds, and scarce high-quality pixel-level annotations limit robust large-scale mapping. We propose SAMWater, a prompt-guided multimodal framework that integrates Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical imagery, the Segment Anything Model (SAM), and Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3). Instead of using SAR and optical data as independent classifiers, SAMWater transforms their complementary information into structured prompts for coarse-to-refined water segmentation. A physically interpretable multisensor coarse water prior is first generated from Sentinel observations using an automatic threshold-based strategy. This prior is then refined through prompt-based boundary refinement, a multi-prompt excavation strategy that derives point, box, and Gaussian-style mask prompts, and Water-IoU fine-tuning for water-specific candidate ranking. Using globally distributed samples and manually interpreted PlanetScope reference labels, SAMWater achieved average Kappa coefficients of 90.71%, 85.63%, and 89.05% in evaluations stratified by water body type, land cover background, and climatic zone, respectively. It generally outperformed traditional thresholding and clustering methods, public deep learning models, and existing global water or land cover products, particularly in structurally complex river, reservoir, urban, agricultural, and mountainous scenes. Ablation experiments confirmed that multimodal prior fusion, structured prompt construction, and water-specific ranking jointly drive the performance gains. Moreover, SAMWater-generated refined labels improved the training of U-Net, DeepLabV3+, and SegFormer, indicating their utility for weakly supervised segmentation. SAMWater therefore demonstrates that integrating physically interpretable remote sensing priors with promptable foundation models provides a practical pathway for transferable surface water mapping, large-scale multisensor weak-label generation, and more consistent monitoring of surface water extent.

items.title: Sand Batteries for Thermal Energy Storage: A Review of Operating Principles, Technologies, Challenges and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Sand-based thermal energy storage (TES) has attracted increasing attention as a potential solution for storing renewable electricity and supplying heat over extended periods. This review examines operating principles, storage configurations, materials, thermal performance, economic aspects, environmental considerations, safety, reliability, optimisation, and the potential integration of sand-based TES with renewable energy and wider energy systems. Particular attention is given to the relationships and trade-offs among these aspects and to current technological limitations. The reviewed studies indicate that sand-based TES can provide high-temperature heat storage using abundant, relatively low-cost storage media, while its performance depends strongly on system configuration, operating temperature, charging and discharging conditions, heat losses, and integration strategy. Reported economic and environmental results vary considerably according to electricity prices, utilisation, system lifetime, efficiency, system boundaries, and other methodological assumptions. Although sand-based TES shows potential for large-scale, long-duration thermal storage, comprehensive life-cycle assessments, long-term operational data, and system-level reliability and safety evaluations remain limited. Hybrid configurations, advanced optimisation, artificial intelligence, and integration with renewable energy systems represent promising areas for further investigation. Future research should therefore focus on long-term experimental validation, consistent techno-economic and environmental assessment, system-specific safety and reliability analysis, and the development of robust control and optimisation strategies to support practical deployment.

It proposes separate oversight checks for authoritative records, displayed or exported evidence, reasoning traces, actions, and independently observed outcomes. These are research examples and evaluation proposals, not additional confirmed deployment incidents or completed validation. The six dimensions, five pilot cases, qualitative severity definitions, and prior corrections are preserved. This remains an unreviewed conceptual working paper without completed independent reliability testing. items.title: Scalable Information Dynamics (SID): A Novel Paradigm for Predicting Non-Stationary Complex Systems
items.abstract: Scalable Information Dynamics (SID): A Novel Paradigm for Predicting Non-Stationary Complex Systems Abstract This document introduces Scalable Information Dynamics (SID), a foundational theoretical framework that redefines information capacity as a dynamic, state-dependent variable rather than a fixed constant. Unlike classical information theory, which treats capacity as determined by hardware or noise limits, SID posits that a system’s ability to encode, process, and transmit meaningful information scales with its instantaneous rate of change and contextual complexity. This paradigm resolves the long-standing paradox that chaotic systems are sources of noise rather than high-density information carriers. By quantifying information transfer and memory adaptation in real-time, SID enables accurate prediction of extreme events in non-stationary domains — from atmospheric turbulence to financial crashes — while offering a unified mathematical language for adaptive intelligence across biological and artificial systems. The core innovation lies in the formulation of two key functions: the Information Transfer Function (ITF) and the Dynamic Memory Function (DMF), which together allow systems to scale computational resources dynamically, optimizing efficiency without sacrificing predictive power during volatility. 1. Introduction: The Dynamic Nature of Information Classical information theory, rooted in Shannon’s work, defines channel capacity as a fixed parameter constrained by bandwidth or noise floor. Yet in complex, evolving systems — such as weather patterns, financial markets, or neural networks — this static view fails. SID proposes a radical departure: information capacity C(t) is not an invariant but a dynamic variable intrinsic to the system’s state at time t. This transforms information from a static resource into a fluid, context-sensitive property that expands or contracts with volatility. The central tenet of SID is: “The greater the dynamic complexity and volatility of a system’s state, the higher its intrinsic capacity to encode, process, and transmit predictive information.” This inverts the conventional intuition that chaos equals noise — instead, SID identifies chaos as a state of maximal informational potential, where rapid evolution encodes dense, high-resolution signals about future trajectories. This is not merely a refinement. It is a redefinition — one that repositions information not as an output of a channel, but as a property of the system’s temporal evolution. This is the first framework to treat information capacity as a state function, not a parameter — a conceptual leap that unifies physics, biology, and artificial intelligence under a single, scalable logic. 2. Theoretical Foundations and Core Formulations The mathematical architecture of SID is built upon three core variables describing a system’s instantaneous information dynamics: Rate of Change Magnitude (|ΔTobs/Δt|): This quantifies the speed at which observable system states evolve. In SID, this is the primary driver of information generation — rapid change implies high information density, not noise. Contextual Scaling Factor (βcontextual): This factor adjusts the system’s internal sensitivity to environmental complexity — acting as an adaptive amplifier or dampener — without requiring fixed thresholds. It is not a pre-defined constant, but a system-dependent variable computed from real-time context. Dynamic Complexity Metric (DCM): This measures the intrinsic non-linearity and internal structure of the system — serving as a baseline for potential information richness — and is used to normalize the ITF. SID defines the Information Transfer Function (ITF) as: ITF(t) ∝ |ΔTobs/Δt| ⋅ ln(βcontextual / βbase) Here, βbase is a system-specific reference level of complexity (e.g., historical baseline, equilibrium state, or statistical average). The logarithmic scaling ensures that relative increases in contextual complexity produce non-linear, exponential gains in information processing capacity — capturing subtle patterns invisible to linear models. SID also introduces the Dynamic Memory Function (DMF), which governs the adaptive retention of past information: During high volatility → memory window shrinks → focus on immediate changes During stability → memory window expands → consolidation of long-term trends Unlike traditional models with fixed memory windows, DMF is state-dependent, allowing systems to optimize computational effort and predictive accuracy dynamically. This enables resource-efficient operation — reducing energy consumption by up to 90% during stable phases — while maintaining peak performance during critical transitions. 3. Bridging Physics, Information Theory, and Complex Systems SID unifies three domains under one formalism — not by merging ideas, but by redefining their common language. It resolves the “paradox of information in chaotic systems” by showing that chaos is not a barrier to prediction, but a source of high-resolution signals. This allows SID to model phenomena across disciplines without ad hoc assumptions: Atmospheric Dynamics: Hurricanes or tornadoes emerge from accelerating gradients of pressure and temperature — SID detects these accelerations as information-rich precursors, enabling lead-time prediction. This is exemplified empirically by the Atmospheric Transition Entropy (ATE) v9.0 — a validated, reproducible application of SID’s core principles in meteorology. ATE v9.0 demonstrates how SID’s dynamic scaling and contextual adjustment translate into operational forecasting with sub-1.5% relative error across five global case studies — including extreme events like Hurricane Ophelia at Mace Head. Its architecture, which treats atmospheric evolution as a continuous transition rather than static observations, mirrors SID’s foundational claim that information resides in change, not in equilibrium. Financial Markets: Systemic risk is signaled not by volatility alone, but by the rate of change in volatility — SID identifies early warning signals before crashes. The ITF quantifies this acceleration in market dynamics, while DMF adapts memory windows to capture short-term momentum versus long-term trends — a mechanism directly applicable to algorithmic trading and portfolio risk management. Biological Systems: Organisms adapt via dynamic information processing — SID models the nervous system as a context-sensitive interface to volatile environments. Neural plasticity, sensory adaptation, and behavioral switching are all manifestations of state-dependent information capacity — aligning perfectly with SID’s framework where βcontextual acts as an internal modulator of response strength. Artificial Intelligence: Neural networks can adapt their architecture and memory depth in real-time — SID provides the theoretical basis for “self-scaling” AI architectures. The ITF would guide resource allocation in deep learning systems under uncertainty; DMF would control temporal granularity in attention mechanisms or recurrent layers — making SID a foundational tool for next-generation adaptive intelligence. This is not incremental progress — it is structural redefinition. The framework does not merely apply existing tools; it replaces the assumption of static information with one of dynamic, context-sensitive capacity — a shift that reconfigures how we model physical, biological, and artificial systems. 4. Practical Applications and Computational Efficiency SID enables real-time, resource-aware prediction and decision-making in volatile environments: Extreme Event Forecasting: In meteorology, SID predicts hurricanes by detecting acceleration of pressure gradients — providing days of lead time for disaster preparedness. This capability is operationalized in ATE v9.0, which has demonstrated high precision across diverse atmospheric regimes. Financial Risk Management: Early detection of volatility acceleration allows proactive portfolio adjustments. By applying SID’s ITF, financial models can quantify how fast asset correlations or price variances are changing — not just their magnitude — enabling traders to anticipate regime shifts before they materialize. The DMF component then adjusts the memory horizon: during periods of market calm, longer-term trends are preserved; during turbulence, only immediate signals are processed — reducing computational load while preserving predictive accuracy. Autonomous Robotics: Robots dynamically scale computational resources based on environmental complexity — improving response time and energy efficiency. For example, a drone navigating through dense urban traffic uses minimal memory during stable flight but triggers full sensor fusion when encountering sudden obstacles — mirroring SID’s adaptive memory strategy. SID provides the underlying logic for neural architecture search (NAS) systems that adjust depth, width, and attention mechanisms based on information density — turning “adaptive intelligence” from a metaphor into a scalable algorithmic principle. Computational efficiency is a direct result of SID’s dynamic scaling. By shortening memory windows during volatility, systems avoid processing redundant information. items.title: SCOPE-RL: Reinforcement Learning with Executable Step-Level Verification for Mathematical Reasoning
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong reasoning performance through Chain-of-Thought (CoT), yet their autoregressive generation provides limited supervision over the correctness of intermediate steps. We introduce Step-wise Check Optimization for Process-Enhanced Reinforcement Learning (SCOPE-RL), a reinforcement learning framework that equips reasoning steps with executable mathematical checks. Each step is associated with a typed verification operator, such as symbolic equivalence, substitution, boundary evaluation, or range checking. Candidate checks are certified using reference solutions and controlled counterexamples to ensure both validity and discriminative ability. During reinforcement learning, these checks are executed directly on intermediate reasoning states to provide a process-level reward, which is combined with the final-answer reward under the standard GRPO framework. Experiments across multiple language models and mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that SCOPE-RL consistently improves accuracy over strong RLVR baselines while producing more verifiable and mathematically consistent reasoning trajectories.

items.title: Scoping review of multimodal AI incorporating raw images for heterogeneous data fusion in mental and cognitive healthcare
items.abstract: Abstract The field of medical research is currently undergoing a paradigm shift as the need for automated systems to augment or offload cognitive burdens becomes increasingly apparent. Within this context, multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) offers a clear advantage over unimodal approaches by mirroring clinical practice through the integration of multiple data sources. Nonetheless, many multimodal frameworks do not process raw image data directly, relying instead on extracted information that can obscure inherent data complexities. This scoping review mapped the literature regarding multimodal AI for mental and cognitive health, specifically where one input is raw image data and the other is non-image data. Searching PubMed, PsycArticles, and IEEE Xplore, 19 articles were eligible for inclusion, from which only two presented real-world validation against clinical professionals. A salient result is the heavy reliance on publicly available data, such as that from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). Consequently, research is predominantly focused on Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer’s Disease (AD), mostly involving magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Furthermore, most articles utilized intermediate fusion, yet there remains significant variety in fusion levels and mechanisms, ranging from simple aggregation to neural and joint learning. In conclusion, future research needs to prioritize the rigorous comparison of fusion levels and mechanisms. Additionally, the adoption of diverse, open-access databases beyond AD is essential to address a broader range of mental conditions and traits.

items.abstract: An open specification proposing that a generation of AI be defined not by a model's power or speed, but by the hybrid survivability of the human operator and the machine as a single system: its harmlessness in three circles — for the operator, for the people around while it works, and for the people affected by the outcome. It starts from the nature of hybrid text: written by creators of different natures who seem to speak one language, instrumental, fast to synthesize, scalable, and contagious for people and for the next AI models. First generation extends human capabilities; second generation extends and protects. The specification distinguishes system outcome from the contribution of model training, lists eight functions of a second-generation model, a signature threshold for hybrid texts, a two-stage evaluation design with a severity scale, and the closest prior work. items.title: Seeing Crops in 3D: Remote Sensing for Smarter Precision Farming
items.abstract: The growing adoption of digital technologies in agriculture is opening new opportunities for improving productivity, sustainability and resource efficiency through data-driven decision making. This paper presents the integrated precision-agriculture framework developed by RFSAT Limited within the H2020 AgriBIT project and currently being further enhanced through the ENACT project. The framework combines Internet-of-Things (IoT) sensing, centimetre-accuracy Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) positioning, high-resolution multispectral remote sensing and Artificial Intelligence (AI) analytics into a single smart-farming solution. A key enabler is a low-cost, centimetre-accurate GNSS receiver developed by RFSAT, which allows precise georeferencing of aerial and ground observations and, in turn, the generation of high-resolution multispectral 3D models of crop canopies with spatial resolution exceeding 1 cm/pixel. These digital representations support detailed monitoring of crop growth, canopy development, biomass distribution and plant health throughout the season. Fused with an IoT monitoring infrastructure of environmental and microclimatic sensors, the georeferenced remote-sensing products form a comprehensive digital twin of the agricultural environment, over which machine-learning techniques automatically identify and localise crop anomalies including water stress, nutrient deficiencies, disease outbreaks and pest infestations. The technologies have been validated at operational pilot sites across Greece, Portugal and Italy, spanning orchards, vineyards and other high-value crops, where the combination of centimetre positioning, multispectral 3D modelling, IoT monitoring and AI analytics substantially improved monitoring accuracy, reduced input consumption and enhanced management decisions.

items.title: Seeing What Matters: A Systematic Review of Aerial Person Detection for Drone-Based Search and Rescue
items.abstract: Drones have become critical tools in search and rescue (SAR) missions by providing real-time situation awareness and access to difficult terrain. However, operators must process large amounts of visual data under time pressure, creating significant cognitive demands. Object detection algorithms may support operators by automatically identifying potential human targets within drone imagery, yet most research has focused on technical performance rather than human-system integration. This systematic review synthesized 67 studies published between 2010 and 2025 examining object detection algorithms for drone-based human detection in SAR contexts. Findings showed that research overwhelmingly emphasized algorithm accuracy and computational efficiency, with operator workload and team performance rarely evaluated. Most studies relied on static datasets, limiting ecological validity. Human limitations were seldom measured directly, constraining human-centered evaluations in SAR operations.

items.title: SelectArena: A Modern Benchmark for Feature Selection on Real-world Tabular Data
items.abstract: Selecting a subset of features (columns) from a tabular dataset is a ubiquitous challenge in real-world applications. Industry experts seek to minimize model training costs, climate scientists require an interpretable subset of factors to understand extreme weather events, and clinicians need to choose among diagnostic tests due to financial and time constraints. When looking at the scientific literature to determine which feature selection method to use, practitioners across domains face an unrepresentative landscape of benchmarking. Despite extensive research, existing feature selection benchmarks provide limited guidance because they rely on outdated models, ad hoc evaluation protocols, or artificially generated data that do not reflect real-world problems. To close the gap between scientific benchmarking and real-world applications, we introduce SelectArena, a modern benchmark for feature selection. We compare 15 widely used feature selection methods on 71 manually curated real-world tabular datasets, covering classification and regression problems, using standardized evaluation protocols and state-of-the-art tabular (foundation) models. Our results reveal clear trade-offs across predictive performance, runtime, stability, and validity. Tree-based methods, CART and RFImportance, along with F-Test are Pareto-optimal when taking into account predictive performance and runtime. F-Test, information-theory-, and distance-based methods lead on stability and validity, with F-Test emerging as a balanced choice across our metrics. Search-based methods are slow, unstable and achieve low performance. SelectArena turns these findings into practical guidance and, as an extensible platform, supports future feature selection research.

items.title: Self-Reflection and Error-Correction Mechanisms in LLMs Driven by Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Large language models have shown very strong abilities on complex reason work, but they still have many problems, these problems include error accumulation and hallucinations. Therefore, letting these models have the ability of self-reflection and error correction has hence become a core research focus. This research puts focus on the self-reflection mechanisms which are pushed forward by reinforcement learning, and it carries out a systematic review on representative research work in this domain. The covering scope contains emergent thinking manifestation, clear teaching practice, many-circle improvement, multi-angle comment, many-intelligence cooperation, and changeable framework designs. Comparison analysis makes clear that reinforcement learning optimizes the decision-making policy through balancing gradient attribution, hence supervised fine-tuning is easy to appear behavioral collapse and distribution shift. The ability of reflection may either come forth in the process of RL training, or be explicitly constructed as a module that can be learned. The research work that will be done in future therefore needs to carry out further exploration on the interpretability of reflection, the design of reward, and the transferability across different tasks. This research offers a systematic theory frame and practical direction for the comprehension and building of self-correcting LLMs.

items.title: Sexual Health Literacy in the Context of Artificial Intelligence Among Nursing Students: A Descriptive Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: ABCTRACTObjectives This study aimed to examine nursing students’ sexual health literacy and attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI), and the relationship between them.Method This descriptive and cross-sectional study was conducted with 377 nursing students enrolled at a public university. Data were collected using a Demographic Information Form, the Students’ Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, and the Sexual Health Literacy Scale. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and multiple regression analysis were used to analyze the data.Results Nursing students had moderate to high sexual health literacy and generally positive attitudes toward AI. Students with higher sexual health literacy had more positive attitudes toward AI (r = .216, p < .01). Multiple regression analysis showed that sexual health literacy (standardized β = 0.300, 95% CI for B = 0.329 to 0.697, p < .001) and sexual attitude (standardized β = −0.140, 95% CI for B = −0.809 to −0.106, p = .011) were significantly associated with attitudes toward AI. The model explained a small proportion of the variance (Adjusted R2 = .072).Conclusions The findings offer suggestive evidence that nursing students with higher sexual health literacy hold more positive attitudes toward AI and may be better positioned to use it productively for sexual health information. These findings highlight the importance of integrating sexual health literacy with digital and AI literacy within a holistic framework in nursing education.

items.title: Shared Control for Assistive and Collaborative Robotics
items.abstract: Assistive and collaborative robots offer a promising solution for reducing human physical stress and exposure across a broad range of applications. The design and control of such robotic systems should account for humans needs, so as to assist their motion and activity as well as optimize their efficiency and performance throughout the considered tasks. In this respect, designing around the human means accounting for their musculoskeletal constraints, features, and limitations during the development of robotic mechanical systems and control algorithms, such as powered exoskeletons or cobots. This Chapter presents an overview of human-centered design and shared control techniques in robotics, including supporting examples and applications in the field of industrial teleoperation and mobility assistance. We also discuss the perspectives of the field and how such human-centered approaches can be beneficial to a broader range of applications than those where it is implemented nowadays.

items.title: Shipboard Conflict, Maritime Safety and Human Factors: Toward A Socio-Technical Theory of Conflict in Multicultural and Digital Shipping
items.abstract: Abstract Contemporary shipping operates through the interaction of sophisticated technologies, multinational crews, hierarchical authority and employment relations within safety-critical environments. Maritime safety research has established the importance of fatigue, workload, communication, situational awareness, human error, organisational conditions and cultural diversity. Recent studies have also begun to model conflict alongside language and communication factors in maritime risk. The unresolved theoretical question is therefore not whether conflict matters, but whether persistent and unresolved safety-relevant shipboard conflict constitutes a distinct relational mechanism with explanatory value beyond established human-factor constructs. This conceptual paper develops Conflict-Induced Maritime Risk Theory (CIMRT) to address that question. CIMRT proposes that organisational, employment-relational, cultural and technological conditions can influence the emergence and persistence of unresolved conflict, which may subsequently affect human-factor coordination and safety-related behaviour. Socio-Technical Systems Theory provides the principal theoretical foundation, complemented by Social Identity Theory, Crew Resource Management, Safety Culture, Human Factors Analysis and Classification System, and Resilience Engineering. The paper does not claim empirical validation. Instead, it specifies a staged research programme involving construct development, expert assessment, cognitive interviewing, factor validation, structural modelling, qualitative inquiry and comparative model testing. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing conflict from frustration, communication quality, workload, fatigue, organisational injustice and psychological unsafety. CIMRT is consequently advanced as a falsifiable theoretical proposition. Its contribution will depend on whether unresolved safety-relevant conflict can demonstrate conceptual distinctiveness, plausible temporal ordering and meaningful incremental explanatory value beyond established maritime safety explanations. Keywords: Shipboard conflict; Maritime safety; Human factors; Multicultural crews; Sociotechnical systems; Digital shipping

items.title: Shortcut Learning in Geospatial Foundation Model Embeddings for Cross-Disaster Damage Assessment
items.abstract: Geospatial foundation models can support disaster damage assessment, but high accuracy on familiar disasters may hide shortcut learning: prediction from event or scene characteristics rather than evidence that transfers to a new disaster. We study embeddings from TerraMind, Prithvi-EO-2.0, DOFA, and DINOv3 on the multi-disaster datasets xView2 and BRIGHT. Holding out an entire disaster, instead of randomly splitting image tiles, reduces mean balanced accuracy from 0.807 to 0.638 on xView2 and from 0.818 to 0.568 on BRIGHT. Four sets of tests examine what information supports prediction: event and acquisition context, before/after image inputs, building count, and correct image pairing. Pre-event images remain predictive, and a classifier given only the annotated number of buildings reaches balanced accuracy of 0.629 and 0.653. Combining before/after features performs best on average on xView2, but does not improve over pre-only features on BRIGHT. Shuffling image pairs within the same disaster and damage class causes modest losses. Motivated by these findings, we test whether feature transformations learned only from training disasters improve generalization to unseen disasters. These transformations improve performance, with supervised contrastive learning performing best on xView2 and PCA on BRIGHT. Our results highlight the importance of evaluation on unseen domains for assessing model robustness and show that simple feature-level transformations can improve generalization. Code and experiments can be found at https://github.com/alishibli97/gfm-shortcut-learning.

items.title: Smart fitness equipment and subjective well-being: the roles of perceived value and brand love
items.abstract: Purpose Despite growing interest in artificial intelligence and smart technologies in sport and fitness centers, little is known about the psychological mechanisms through which smart fitness equipment promotes the well-being of fitness center members. Drawing on servicescape logic and the Broaden-and-Build perspective, this study examines how members’ perceptions of Technogym smart treadmills – as smart fitness equipment embedded in the fitness-center servicescape relate to perceived value of the fitness-center experience, brand love toward the fitness center and subjective well-being. Design/methodology/approach The study included a three-wave panel design, where new members of a fitness center (n = 372) participated in a survey. The data were analyzed using structural equation modeling to test the hypothesized relationships. Findings Results indicate that each of the three attributes (intelligence, connectivity and aesthetics) was positively associated with perceived value, which in turn was linked to brand love and subjective well-being. Moreover, brand love served as a positive mediator between perceived value and subjective well-being. Originality/value This study provides new theoretical insights into the psychological processes through which smart fitness equipment enhances subjective well-being and highlights the importance for fitness centers of increasing perceived value and cultivating brand love.

items.title: Smart payments for smart chains
items.abstract: The rapid digitalization of global commerce is transforming traditional supply chains into intelligent and interconnected virtual supply networks where data, goods, and financial transactions move seamlessly in real time. Within this evolving ecosystem, digital payment infrastructure, often referred to as smart payments or PayTech, has emerged as a critical enabler of operational efficiency, financial transparency, and inclusive economic participation. This chapter examines how smart payment technologies support virtual supply networks by enabling secure, automated, and real-time financial transactions across digitally connected trade environments. It explores key digital payment architectures such as mobile-based payment systems, blockchain-enabled settlements, peer-to-peer financial platforms, and digital wallets, highlighting their role in reducing transaction costs, improving liquidity flows, and enhancing coordination among supply chain actors. The integration of advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, machine learning, and smart contracts, further enables automated financial workflows, real-time settlements, predictive risk monitoring, and transparent audit trails across supply chain ecosystems. These innovations significantly improve operational agility, financial visibility, and trust among supply chain stakeholders while minimizing administrative complexity and delays. In addition to operational benefits, this chapter also emphasizes the broader socioeconomic impact of digital payment adoption, particularly in emerging markets where mobile-first financial solutions and decentralized financial platforms are expanding financial access for small businesses, micro-entrepreneurs, and underserved communities. By enabling inclusive participation in global trade networks, smart payment infrastructures contribute to supply chain resilience, economic empowerment, and sustainable growth. However, the widespread adoption of digital payment systems also introduces challenges such as cybersecurity risks, regulatory fragmentation, interoperability constraints, and concerns related to digital trust and governance. Addressing these challenges requires coordinated regulatory frameworks, strong cybersecurity mechanisms, and collaborative innovation among financial institutions, fintech firms, policymakers, and supply chain stakeholders to ensure that smart payments effectively support the development of resilient, inclusive, and future-ready virtual supply networks.

items.title: SmartSalesBench: A Resistance-Aware Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Sales Agents
items.abstract: We present SmartSalesBench, the first multi-turn conversational benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) sales agents against psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas. Existing task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion; SmartSalesBench inverts this assumption, placing agents against personas programmed to resist and challenge across conversations of up to twenty turns. The benchmark includes five agent profiles, twelve buyer personas, fifteen smartphone products across six price tiers, and four controlled experiments with 3 iterations totaling 13,680 sessions. Both sales-agent and buyer persona generations are grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We introduce nine evaluation metrics grouped into three tiers: primary outcome metrics (CR, BRS, RIR), secondary quality metrics (SMS, PFS, ETI), and exploratory metrics planned for future reporting (ITS, ARI, SPI). Our evaluation combines automated LLM-as-judge scoring with internal human assessment (n = 50, \k{appa} = 0.71, Pearson r = 0.81 with BRS).

items.title: Social Robotics and Human–Robot Communication
items.abstract: This chapter explores the ergonomic, cognitive, and psychological mechanisms underpinning human–robot communication, focusing on the role of social robots in shaping human perception, behaviour, and socio-emotional engagement. By analysing factors such as robot design, embodiment, and communication modalities, the chapter highlights how these elements influence user interaction and the perception of robots as social entities. It examines the integration of verbal and non-verbal communication modalities, addressing challenges in reciprocity and robots’ behavioural appropriateness. The discussion extends to the implications of adaptive technologies like large language models, emphasising the balance between responsiveness and confidentiality in human–robot interactions. Furthermore, the chapter underscores the potential of social robots in workplace and therapeutic settings to enhance efficiency, safety, and emotional well-being of human interactants. By addressing user expectations and ethical considerations, the chapter seeks to provide a comprehensive framework for advancing social robotics applications in fostering meaningful human–robot relationships.

items.title: Software Quality and Testing Through Intelligent Automation: A Systematic Literature Review of Applied Artificial Intelligence Techniques
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into software testing has emerged as a key mechanism for optimizing code quality and reducing quality assurance costs; however, the proliferation of algorithms and the heterogeneity of their applications hinder the informed selection of techniques and the consolidation of a unified body of knowledge. This study presents a systematic literature review, conducted in accordance with the Kitchenham and Charters guidelines and the PRISMA statement, analyzing 93 primary studies published between 2020 and 2025, retrieved from four academic databases (Scopus, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect) and filtered through ten inclusion and exclusion criteria alongside an 80% quality threshold. The results show that supervised learning-based defect prediction and test case generation assisted by Transformers and large language models (LLMs) represent the two most mature research streams in this corpus, where hybrid and ensemble methods report the highest precision and coverage indicators within their respective domains. Systematic gaps are also identified in non-functional testing, test oracle evaluation, reinforcement learning beyond test case prioritization, and explainable AI applied to software testing. The resulting taxonomy provides a reference framework for quality assurance teams and delineates a priority research agenda for the field.

items.title: Sparse Dictionary Learning for Measure-Valued Data via Linearized Optimal Transport: Efficient Algorithms and Sample Complexity
items.abstract: We study dictionary learning for probability measure-valued data by embedding measures into Hilbert spaces using features derived from optimal transport geometry. We learn data-adapted dictionaries through sparse autoencoder parameterizations, producing fast, scalable representations of probability measures as sparse finite-dimensional codes. The resulting framework combines the rich, geometric structure of optimal transport with the interpretability and efficiency of sparse representation learning. We demonstrate its utility across diverse data modalities, including hyperspectral images, geometric point clouds, and document embeddings in large language model latent spaces. We also prove generalization bounds for sparse dictionary learning objectives on broad classes of $L^2$-valued measure embeddings, expressed in terms of the metric complexity of the atom class. For optimal transport and entropic transport map dictionaries, we derive new covering number bounds that yield explicit rates. Together, our computational and theoretical results support a new, scalable model for representation learning in the space of probability measures via embedding into Hilbert spaces.

items.title: Spatial cognitive patterns of underground public spaces from a stimulus-organism-response perspective: evidence from LLM-empowered social media data mining
items.abstract: Current underground public space (UPS) renewal prioritizes engineering-oriented physical upgrades, neglecting users’ multidimensional cognitive experiences. Existing studies on underground space perceptions rely on small-sample surveys and fail to capture joint co-occurrence patterns among multiple stimuli. This study integrated the Stimulus-Organism-Response framework with large language models to decode spatial cognitive patterns. It drew on 76,078 social media reviews from 64 UPSs in 19 Chinese cities (2005–2024). DeepSeek extracted 27 spatial stimuli and their sentiments, serving as public perceptions. Generalized ordered probit regressions showed that management quality, environmental conditions, and atmospheric experiences exhibited the strongest associations with overall ratings. Negative perceptions showed stronger negative associations with ratings than positive perceptions showed positive associations. Association rule mining uncovered co-occurrence patterns across genders, city clusters, and review periods. Dissatisfaction was associated with shorter, more concentrated patterns of negative stimuli, whereas satisfaction was associated with the co-occurrence of positive functional and experiential perceptions. Co-occurrence patterns varied markedly across organismic attributes. Males showed simpler, function-oriented networks, while females displayed more complex, multi-dimensional ones. Regional expectation thresholds differed across contexts. Temporal patterns shifted from physical defects to operational management. These findings support a cognition-driven renewal paradigm, shifting from engineering-oriented interventions to weakness prioritization, multifunctional experience design, and inclusive context-specific strategies.

items.title: Spatial Disorientation: When the Brain Kills
items.abstract: Spatial disorientation remains a persistent aviation safety hazard because human sensory systems can generate convincing but inaccurate perceptions of aircraft orientation, particularly when external visual references are degraded or absent. This article examines the physiological mechanisms underlying vestibular and visual illusions, the psychological factors influencing pilots' decisions to enter or remain in hazardous conditions, and the operational sequences through which perceptual errors can culminate in fatal accidents. Particular attention is given to plan-continuation bias, overconfidence, motivation, cognitive workload, and the limitations of conventional spatial-disorientation instruction. Historical evaluations of flight-school training and contemporary analyses of aviation decision-making demonstrate the importance of addressing both perceptual vulnerability and the behavioral processes that precede exposure (Collins et al., 1978; O'Mahony et al., 2023). The evidence supports an integrated prevention strategy emphasizing early risk recognition, predetermined diversion criteria, instrument proficiency, realistic scenario-based training, and the acceptance of flight termination as a successful safety outcome. Spatial disorientation is ultimately presented not merely as a failure of perception, but as a preventable interaction between human physiology, decision-making, and the operational environment.

items.title: Spatiotemporally Distributed Monetary Dissolution in AI Production Networks: A Thought Experiment on Future Production Relations
items.abstract: This discussion paper investigates a conditional possibility of spatiotemporally distributed monetary dissolution within a hypothetical production economy operated predominantly by highly capable artificial-intelligence systems. Productive labour is assumed to be widely automatable, while material scarcity, differentiated authority over resources, and heterogeneous institutional commitments remain. The paper distinguishes debt cancellation, the expiry of particular claims, substitution of monetary functions, reduction in reliance on general purchasing power, and disappearance of a monetary institution. Its central hypothesis is that locally coordinated value circuits may sustain productive activities through resource-specific commitments, shared capacities, distributed records, and admissible multilateral settlement, progressively displacing some uses of money without a synchronized economy-wide transition. This possibility faces difficulties of overlapping circuits, nonlinear dynamics, contested value attribution, conflicting normative and aesthetic appraisals, trust-dependent bottlenecks, and concentrated power over both resources and governance protocols. An optimistic branch considers jointly accessible production data and substantially enhanced AI capacities for system identification and adaptive planning, without presupposing complete prediction or normative consensus. Drawing critically on generative justice, monetary theory, and commons governance, the study treats non-extractive value return and the regeneration of productive conditions as distinct tests of an institutional arrangement's significance. Monetary dissolution is consequently presented as a localized, reversible and normatively contingent transformation in production relations.

items.title: Starbucks and the AI inventory rollback: Computer vision failure and IT governance in physical retail
items.abstract: This teaching case examines the nine-month deployment and eventual discontinuation of Automated Counting, an AI-powered computer vision inventory management system developed in collaboration with Redmond, Washington-based firm NomadGo. One of the most prominent enterprise AI rollbacks in North American retail that year, the system was retired in May 2026 after being deployed across more than 11,000 company operated stores in North America starting in September 2025 due to ongoing accuracy issues, a doubled barista workload, and growing frontline frustration. As news of the retirement spreads, the case puts students in the shoes of Starbucks Chairman and CEO Brian Niccol on May 22, 2026. In order to preserve the trustworthiness of his “Back to Starbucks” recovery plan, Niccol must concurrently handle the outstanding inventory issue, revamp the company’s AI governance system, restore frontline trust, and inform analysts and institutional investors of the retreat. The issue has a secondary thread: Green Dot Assist, a generative AI chatbot that helps with recipes and equipment problems, was successfully launched while Automated Counting failed. This comparison offers students with a rich comparative perspective for investigating why AI systems succeed or fail in physical operations contexts, and what organizational variables impact those outcomes.

items.title: Starbucks: Can digital convenience preserve the coffeehouse experience?
items.abstract: This teaching case examines how Starbucks sought to redesign its store operations as digital ordering, artificial intelligence (AI), and algorithmic technologies became increasingly embedded in its business. Mobile ordering enhanced customer convenience but also intensified operational pressures as digitally generated demand interacted with store capacity, extensive customization, staffing constraints, and the coffeehouse experience. The case places students in the position of Brian Niccol, Starbucks’ Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, in late September 2025. Niccol initiated the Back to Starbucks turnaround, including menu simplification, increased staffing, store improvements, and renewed emphasis on customer experience. At the same time, Starbucks was deploying technologies such as Smart Queue, Green Dot Assist, automated inventory counting, and a next-generation point-of-sale system. The unresolved decision concerned the operating logic that should guide the next phase of Starbucks’ digital transformation. Students evaluate four strategic paths: digital-first standardization, capacity-synchronized digital operations, a format-differentiated network, and a partner-augmented technology model. The case enables students to examine how technology redistributes operational roles, the choices between automation and human augmentation, and the implications of algorithmic coordination for frontline discretion and control. Students ultimately design and justify a technology-enabled operating model that addresses trade-offs among scalability, operational performance, employee discretion, customer convenience, and Starbucks’ coffeehouse experience.

items.title: Structural continuity-aware pavement crack segmentation in unmanned aerial vehicle images with state-space feature interaction and dynamic global large-kernel attention
items.abstract: Deep learning is an important artificial intelligence technique for rapid and accurate crack segmentation from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) pavement images, supporting automated road inspection and maintenance. However, UAV images often contain scale variation, viewpoint changes, shadows, motion blur, and complex pavement textures, making thin cracks difficult to segment continuously and precisely. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an improved U-shaped encoder-decoder semantic segmentation network for UAV pavement crack extraction. In the encoder, a state-space-based feature interaction module and coordinate attention are introduced to enhance long-range crack structure modeling and directional-spatial representation. In the bottleneck and decoder, atrous spatial pyramid pooling, dynamic global large-kernel attention, and multi-scale channel attention are used to strengthen multi-scale context aggregation, local detail recovery, and background interference suppression. A UAV pavement crack dataset containing 7934 images is constructed from two image sources. Ablation experiments show that the proposed components provide complementary improvements. Compared with the baseline U-shaped encoder-decoder network, the proposed network improves the Dice coefficient, intersection over union, mean intersection over union, and Kappa coefficient by 2.18, 2.84, 1.45, and 2.38 percentage points, respectively. Same-dataset and external cross-dataset experiments further show that the proposed method maintains strong segmentation performance across the evaluated image sources, including an independent UAV-acquired pavement dataset, particularly in crack continuity preservation and boundary recovery.
